newsitem.title: INDIA: India sets tax breaks to boost private phone firms.
newsitem.headline: India sets tax breaks to boost private phone firms.

text.p: India, aiming to help fledgling private telephone companies, said on Thursday it would treat telecommunication companies as infrastructure firms and offer them a five-year tax holiday and import duty concessions.

Telecommunication companies would also be entitled to higher foreign commercial borrowing limits of 50 percent of project costs compared with 35 percent at present, the Finance Ministry said in a statement.

The move cleared the air for private telephone companies to work out financial plans after they were set up in India with foreign investment under an economic reform programme that ended a state monopoly on telecommunications.

"Telecom will be treated as infrastructure and all fiscal benefits like tax holiday, concessional project import duty etc., now being made available to the power sector will be extended to the telecom sector also," the statement said.
India currently offers a uniform 20 percent import duty on power equipment.
Power generation companies also enjoy an exemption from income tax for the first five years and 30 percent of their profits are exempted from taxation for an additional five years.
Last year, India began awarding 15-year licences to private companies to set up basic telephone services to end a chronic telephone line shortage and a waiting list of two million.
India, aiming to double the telephone density from one per 100 people to two, estimates it needs an investment of 400 billion rupees ($11.1 billion) to achieve this.
The fiscal incentives would be available to both mobile phone companies and basic telephone service providers, the statement added.

"We definitely see this as a positive step. We see things coming to fruition," said Rajan Mathews, president and chief executive officer of Birla AT&T Ltd, a joint venture between India's Aditya Birla group, which holds 51 percent, and U.S. firm AT&T, which holds 49 percent.
Birla AT&T is setting up mobile telephone services in the western states of Maharashtra and Gujarat at a project cost of around $1.5 billion.
Mathews told Reuters that a 20 percent concessional duty was not expected to be across the board.
He said he expected the average import duty on equipment to come down to 30-35 percent from 80-85 percent following the fiscal incentives announced on Thursday.

"It means a lot more capital for you. It reduces the borrowing amount from financial institutions," Mathews said. But he added that the tax incentives needed parliamentary approval as part of budgetary changes.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is expected to present the budget for 1997/98 (April-March) on February 28.

Among steps to boost the telecom sector listed by the ministry statement were the setting up of an independent Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) and an agreement between the government and financial institutions on assignability of licences.

Assignability of licences would enable bankers to assign a telephone service licence to another firm if an operator fails to honour financial commitments. The TRAI would regulate competition and pricing of telephone services.
